# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–19 (Complete – Updated 142)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fifth year** (Chapter 19). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; collapses after heavy drinking, becomes helpless "whimpering old idiot," dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Within three-to-four days of inheriting, Pitt determines to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies (described with autumn details: frost silvering hedges, light going early, rain threatening after thaw, ruts and puddles). Body of late Sir Pitt lies in apartment, watched unceasingly by professional attendants. **Funeral period activities**: Daily routines include bells ringing to meals and prayers, young ladies' pianoforte instruction by Rebecca, thick-shoed walks in park and village cottages delivering medicine and tracts; evening singing of Handel and Haydn; large worsted work. Pitt accompanies Rawdon and Rebecca to Mudbury with four horses in carriage after baggage sent by cart with loads of game.
- **Year 1818 (referenced in Chapter 19)**: Miss Osborne receives drawing lessons from Mr. Smee, portrait-painter and R.A.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City, Piccadilly, Bowls's lodging-house, Berkeley Square, Roehampton, Bloomsbury Square, Bedford Row, Upper Bedford Place, Bedford Square), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calaus, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender, May Fair, Chapel in May Fair, Cape Town, Finchley Common, Mirecombe, Gaunt Street (Pitt's family house being repaired and beautified for future London meetings), St. George's Hanover Square (Fred Bullock's wedding venue), Lombard Street, Cornhill, Mincing Lane, Ireland, County Cork.

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED (Summer 1816)**
- Nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago. Final days: collapsed after heavy rum-and-water drinking; became helpless "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." Died summer 1816. **Funeral and legacy (Chapter 19)**: Body placed in apartment at Queen's Crawley, watched unceasingly by professional attendants with lights perpetually burning; coffin at end of passage; children avoided the room; elaborate funeral ceremony in autumn; buried in family crypt. **Mourning assessment**: No regrets attended him save from poor woman (Miss Horrocks) who hoped to be his wife and widow and fled in disgrace. Had favorite old pointer; no other friends—forgotten within weeks, "like the kindest and best of us."

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP (Chapter 18-19)**
- Upon father's death: immediately plans to clear estate with ready money. Within three-to-four days, bearing changed; fixes plans to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be on friendliest terms with blood relations. Called Lady Southdown "Lady Macbeth"; when she waited for weakness, rose scared and left library. Told her she won't go away; she let house at Brighton, spent dividends. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Heightened colour; shook Rawdon by hand; saluted Rebecca with handshake and low bow. Has gotten fat; doing the thing handsomely (per Rawdon's assessment). **Toward Rebecca**: Remembered her testimonies of respect and veneration from early days; disposed favorably. Acknowledged marriage improved Rawdon; owned he owed his fortune to it; smiled inwardly as cunning diplomatist recognizing lucky union. Third day after funeral at dinner: actually said to Rebecca, "Ahem! Rebecca, may I give you a wing?"—speech that made her eyes sparkle with pleasure. **Farewell (Chapter 19)**: Accompanied Rawdon and Rebecca to Mudbury with four horses in carriage; bade her farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London at Gaunt Street after house repaired and beautified.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 18-19)**
- Upon Pitt's letter (Chapter 18): but half-pleased. **Wife's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Rebecca tells him she means for him to get Parliament seat, for herself Court presentation, for him place through Lord Steyne's influence. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: Turned red passing through old hall with Rebecca, arm in arm. Abashed; recollections of boyhood, innocence, Eton, mother, dead sister he was passionately fond of. Encouraged by Lady Jane's affection, twirled mustachios and saluted her with kiss, causing her to blush exceedingly. Called her "dev'lish nice little woman." Agreed with Rebecca that Pitt got fat and doing thing handsomely. Upon return to May Fair: exploded with loud laughter when Rebecca described her victorious handling of Lady Southdown's medicine; enjoyed the entertainment with Lord Steyne and son in London. Reported as improved by marriage in habits and demeanor. **Departure (Chapter 19)**: Receives farewell from Pitt, warm greetings from Lady Jane; travels to Mudbury with Rebecca in carriage with four horses and baggage sent by cart.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Character and social position (Chapter 18)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; displays herself at gatherings; sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. Manipulates husband through derision. **Chapter 19 funeral and Queen's Crawley period**: Somewhat pale passing through old hall; pinched husband's arm entering oak parlour. **With Lady Jane**: Lady Jane's embrace brought tears to eyes of "little adventuress"—which ornaments she wore very seldom. Artless mark of kindness and confidence touched and pleased her. Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Lady Jane informed Sir Pitt she thought Rebecca kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With sisters-in-law**: Did not attempt to forget former position of Governess; recalled it frankly and kindly; asked about studies with great gravity; told them she thought of them many days and longed to know of welfare. **With Lady Southdown**: Attacked her on nursery question; claimed her own little boy was saved by calomel; mentioned hearing of her from Reverend Lawrence Grills of chapel in May Fair which she frequented; described how views changed by circumstances; described indebtedness to Mr. Crawley for religious instruction; touched upon Washerwoman of Finchley Common; asked about Lady Emily, now Lady Emily Hornblower at Cape Town. After funeral: felt very agitated and unwell; requested Lady Southdown's medical advice. Lady Southdown came privately at night with parcel of favorite tracts and medicine. Rebecca accepted tracts and medicine, engaged Dowager in conversation about them and welfare of soul to escape medication. After exhausting religious topics, Lady Macbeth would not quit Rebecca's chamber until cup of night-drink was emptied; Rebecca compelled to assume look of gratitude and swallow medicine under Dowager's unyielding nose. Upon return to May Fair: countenance very queer when Rawdon heard what happened; described occurrence with fun she could not disguise. Acted whole scene for Lord Steyne and son: put on night-cap and gown, preached great sermon in serious manner, lectured on virtue of medicine with perfect imitation of Countess's Roman nose. "Give us Lady Southdown and the black dose" became constant cry in her little drawing-room in May Fair. First time: Dowager Countess of Southdown was made amusing. **Queen's Crawley reflections (Chapter 19)**: Carefully revisited old haunts, fields, woods, copses, ponds, gardens, rooms where she spent couple of years seven years ago. Remembered her thoughts and feelings seven years back, contrasted them with present now that she had seen the world and lived with great people and raised herself far beyond original humble station. **Inner assessment (Chapter 19)**: "I have passed beyond it, because I have brains," Becky thought, "and almost all the rest of the world are fools. I could not go back and consort with those people now, whom I used to meet in my father's studio. Lords come up to my door with stars and garters, instead of poor artists with screws of tobacco in their pockets. I have a gentleman for my husband, and an Earl's daughter for my sister, in the very house where I was little better than a servant a few years ago. But am I much better to do now in the world than I was when I was the poor painter's daughter and wheedled the grocer round the corner for sugar and tea? Suppose I had married Francis who was so fond of me--I couldn't have been much poorer than I am now. Heigho! I wish I could exchange my position in society, and all my relations for a snug sum in the Three Per Cent. Consols." **Moral reflections (Chapter 19)**: May have struck her that to have been honest and humble, to have done her duty, and to have marched straightforward on her way, would have brought her as near happiness as the path by which she was striving. But just as the children at Queen's Crawley went round the room where body of their father lay, if ever Becky had these thoughts, she was accustomed to walk round them and not look in. She eluded them and despised them—or at least she was committed to the other path from which retreat was now impossible. **Queen's Crawley routines (Chapter 19)**: Gave pianoforte instruction to young ladies after breakfast; walked in park and shrubberies or beyond palings into village, descending upon cottages with Lady Southdown's medicine and tracts; rode in pony-chaise beside Dowager, listening to her solemn talk with utmost interest; sang Handel and Haydn to family of evenings; engaged in large piece of worsted work, as if born to the business and as if life was to continue until she should sink to grave in polite old age, leaving regrets and great quantity of consols behind her—"as if there were not cares and duns, schemes, shifts, and poverty waiting outside the park gates, to pounce upon her when she issued into the world again." **Departure (Chapter 19)**: Made as many friends of the Mammon of Unrighteousness as she could possibly bring under control. Lady Jane and her husband bade her farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London. Lady Southdown made her up a packet of medicine and sent letter by her to Rev. Lawrence Grills, exhorting him to save the "brand" who honoured the letter from the burning. "Oh so happy!" said Rebecca, throwing up the green eyes. She was immensely happy to be free of the place, and yet loath to go.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapter 18-19)**
- London period (Chapter 18): Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen, scarcely noticed by mother; passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. Relationship with father unchanged: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews mornings during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books; walls covered with pictures. Takes accustomed morning walks with father and pony.

**Miss Briggs (Chapter 19)**
- Background: Miss Crawley's faithful retainer for score of years; received little annuity from Miss Crawley's legacy. **Dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Lady Southdown dismissed her as quickly as decency permitted; Mr. Pitt made no objection. **Post-dismissal and reunion (Chapter 19)**: Fatigued from weary walk to Times Office in City inserting advertisement for sixth time; reached Mr. Bowls's door where she lodged. Rebecca recognizes her, pulls up carriage, embraces warmly. They retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour; Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Briggs told all her history amidst sobs and wonder; Rebecca gave narrative with artlessness and candour. **Mrs. Bowls's warning**: Cautioned Briggs against venturing into "lion's den." Briggs promised to be cautious. **Outcome**: Briggs went to live with Mrs. Rawdon next week; within six months lent Rawdon Crawley six hundred pounds upon annuity.

**Lady Jane Crawley (now Lady Pitt) (Chapter 19)**
- At funeral (Chapter 19): In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Takes both hands of sister-in-law and kisses her affectionately. Embrace brought tears to Rebecca's eyes. Blushes exceedingly when Rawdon salutes her with kiss. Called "dev'lish nice little woman" by Rawdon. **With Rebecca**: Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Engaged in confidential medical conversation about children and ailments. Informed Sir Pitt she thought her new sister-in-law kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With mother**: Busy with her nursery as far as mother would let her; sighs wishing mother would not insist on giving so much medicine; often thinks they should all be better without it. **Farewell (Chapter 19)**: Bade Rebecca farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London.

**Lady Southdown (Dowager Countess) (Chapter 19)**
- Funeral occasion: Preserves solemn stony silence in company of Pitt and rebellious wife; frightens children in nursery with ghastly gloom. Only faint head-dress bending welcomed Rawdon and Rebecca. **With Rebecca**: Comes privately at night in bed-gown looking more like Lady Macbeth than ever; brings parcel of favorite tracts and medicine of her own composition; insists Rebecca take it; will not quit chamber until cup of night-drink is emptied. Later becomes subject of mockery and entertainment in Rebecca's drawing-room in May Fair; made amusing for first time in her life through Rebecca's imitations. **Departure**: Made up a packet of medicine and sent letter by Rebecca to Rev. Lawrence Grills, exhorting him to save the "brand" from the burning.

**Rosalind and Violet (Pitt's sisters) (Chapter 19)**
- Young women summoned from school for funeral. **Rosalind**: Replies with great liberality that person can't help their birth; agrees with brother Pitt that as Rebecca is in family, they are bound to notice her; notes Aunt Bute wants to marry Kate to young Hooper, wine-merchant. **Violet**: Refuses to read Washerwoman of Finchley Common; avoids passage at end of which coffin placed with watchers and lights; comes down to family dinner.

**Fred Bullock and Maria Osborne (Chapter 19)**
- **Marriage negotiations**: Fred's father and senior partners counselled him to take Maria, even with twenty thousand settled, half down, and half at death of Mr. Osborne. Fred "knuckled down" and sent old Hulker with peaceable overtures to Osborne. Excuse was sulkily accepted by Mr. Osborne. **Hulker and Bullock status**: High family of City aristocracy, connected with "nobs" at West End. It was something for old man (Mr. Osborne) to say his son was of the house of Hulker, Bullock, and Co., and his daughter's cousin, Lady Mary Mango, daughter of the Right Hon. The Earl of Castlemouldy. In his imagination he saw his house peopled by the "nobs." So he forgave young Bullock and consented that marriage should take place. **Wedding (Chapter 19)**: Grand affair with breakfast given by bridegroom's relatives near St. George's, Hanover Square. "Nobs of the West End" invited; many signed book. Attendees included: Mr. Mango and Lady Mary Mango with dear young Gwendoline and Guinever Mango as bridesmaids; Colonel Bludyer of Dragoon Guards (eldest son of house of Bludyer Brothers, Mincing Lane), another cousin of bridegroom, and Honourable Mrs. Bludyer; Honourable George Boulter, Lord Levant's son, and his lady, Miss Mango that was; Lord Viscount Castletoddy; Honourable James McMull and Mrs. McMull (formerly Miss Swartz); host of fashionables. **Post-marriage life**: Young couple have house near Berkeley Square and small villa at Roehampton, among the banking colony there. **Maria's conduct and consequences**: Fred was considered to have made rather a mesalliance by the ladies of his family, whose grandfather had been in a Charity School, and who were allied through the husbands with some of the best blood in England. Maria was bound, by superior pride and great care in composition of her visiting-book, to make up for the defects of birth, and felt it her duty to see her father and sister as little as possible. Fred would never allow her to utterly break with old man, who had still so many scores of thousand pounds to give away. But she was still young and incapable of hiding her feelings; and by inviting her papa and sister to her third-rate parties, and behaving very coldly to them when they came, and by avoiding Russell Square, and indiscreetly begging her father to quit that odious vulgar place, she did more harm than all Frederick's diplomacy could repair, and perilled her chance of her inheritance like a giddy heedless creature as she was. **First child**: When Mrs. Frederick's first-born, Frederick Augustus Howard Stanley Devereux Bullock, was born, old Osborne, who was invited to the christening and to be godfather, contented himself with sending the child a gold cup, with twenty guineas inside it for the nurse. "That's more than any of your Lords will give, I'LL warrant," he said and refused to attend at the ceremony. **Jane Osborne's concurrence**: Jane Osborne could not but concur in these opinions respecting her sister's conduct.

**Mr. Osborne (Old) (Chapter 19)**
- **Domestic life**: At five o'clock Mr. Osborne came back to his dinner, which he and his daughter Jane took in silence (seldom broken, except when he swore and was savage, if the cooking was not to his liking), or which they shared twice in a month with a party of dismal friends of Osborne's rank and age. Old Dr. Gulp and his lady from Bloomsbury Square; old Mr. Frowser, the attorney, from Bedford Row, a very great man, and from his business, hand-in-glove with the "nobs at the West End"; old Colonel Livermore, of the Bombay Army, and Mrs. Livermore, from Upper Bedford Place; old Sergeant Toffy and Mrs. Toffy; and sometimes old Sir Thomas Coffin and Lady Coffin, from Bedford Square. Sir Thomas was celebrated as a hanging judge, and the particular tawny port was produced when he dined with Mr. Osborne. These people and their like gave the pompous Russell Square merchant pompous dinners back again. They had solemn rubbers of whist, when they went upstairs after drinking, and their carriages were called at half past ten. Many rich people, whom we poor devils are in the habit of envying, lead contentedly an existence like that above described.

**Jane Osborne (Chapter 19)**
- **Circumstance of seclusion**: Jane Osborne scarcely ever met a man under sixty, and almost the only bachelor who appeared in their society was Mr. Smirk, the celebrated ladies' doctor. **Secret in Jane's life**: There had been a secret in poor Jane's life which had made her father more savage and morose than even nature, pride, and over-feeding had made him. This secret was connected with Miss Wirt, who had a cousin an artist, Mr. Smee, very celebrated since as a portrait-painter and R.A., but who once was glad enough to give drawing lessons to ladies of fashion. Mr. Smee has forgotten where Russell Square is now, but he was glad enough to visit it in the year 1818, when Miss Osborne had instruction from him. **Aftermath**: Jane Osborne kept her bedroom for many days. She was not allowed to have a companion afterwards. Her father swore to her that she should not have a shilling of his money if she made any match without his concurrence; and as he wanted a woman to keep his house, he did not choose that she should marry, so that she was obliged to give up all projects with which Cupid had any share. During her papa's life, then, she resigned herself to the manner of existence here described, and was content to be an old maid. Her sister, meanwhile, was having children with finer names every year and the intercourse between the two grew fainter continually. "Jane and I do not move in the same sphere of life," Mrs. Bullock said. "I regard her as a sister, of course"--which means--what does it mean when a lady says that she regards Jane as a sister?

**Major Dobbin and Mrs. O'Dowd (Chapter 19)**
- **Mrs. O'Dowd's plan**: Among other points, she had made up her mind that Glorvina should marry our old friend Dobbin. Mrs. O'Dowd knew the Major's expectations and appreciated his good qualities and the high character which he enjoyed in his profession. Glorvina, a very handsome, fresh-coloured, black-haired, blue-eyed young lady, who could ride a horse, or play a sonata with any girl out of the County Cork, seemed to be the very person destined to insure Dobbin's happiness—much more than that poor good little weak-spur'ted Amelia, about whom he used to take on so. "Look at Glorvina enter a room," Mrs. O'Dowd would say, "and compare her with that poor Mrs. Osborne, who couldn't say boo to a goose. She'd be worthy of you, Major--you're a quiet man yourself, and want some one to talk for ye. And though she does not come of such good blood as the Malonys or Molloys, let me tell ye, she's of an ancient family that any nobleman might be proud to marry into." **Outcome (Chapter 19)**: Glorvina cried with rage at the failure. She had set her mind on the Major "more than on any of the others," she owned, sobbing. "He'll break my heart, he will, Peggy," she would whimper to her sister-in-law when they were good friends; "sure every one of me frocks must be taken in--it's such a skeleton I'm growing." Fat or thin, laughing or melancholy, on horseback or the music-stool, it was all the same to the Major. And the Colonel, puffing his pipe and listening to these complaints, would suggest that Glory should have some black frocks out in the next box from London, and told a mysterious story of a lady in Ireland who died of grief for the loss of her husband before she got ere a one. **Amelia's letter (Chapter 19)**: Amelia wrote to Dobbin congratulating him with great candour and cordiality upon his approaching nuptials with Miss O'Dowd. "Your sister has just kindly visited me," Amelia wrote in her letter, "and informed me of an INTERESTING EVENT, upon which I beg to offer my MOST SINCERE CONGRATULATIONS. I hope the young lady to whom I hear you are to be UNITED will in every respect prove worthy of one who is himself all kindness and goodness. The poor widow has only her prayers to offer and her cordial cordial wishes for YOUR PROSPERITY! Georgy sends his love to HIS DEAR GODPAPA and hopes that you will not forget him. I tell him that you are about to form OTHER TIES, with one who I am sure merits ALL YOUR AFFECTION, but that, although such ties must of course be the strongest and most sacred, and supersede ALL OTHERS, yet that I am sure the widow and the child whom you have ever protected and loved will always HAVE A CORNER IN YOUR HEART." The letter went on in this strain, protesting throughout as to the extreme satisfaction of the writer. **Emotional state**: So these two were each exemplifying the Vanity of this life, and each longing for what he or she could not get. So both Dobbin and Glorvina are shown to be unfulfilled in their desires.

**Other Characters Status**: Bowls and Firkin (received legacies, married, set up lodging-house); Mrs. Bowls cautious of Rebecca; Colonel Dobbin, Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Lord Steyne, Reverend Bute Crawley, James Crawley, Miss Horrocks (married to saddler at Mudbury, fled in disgrace after hoping to be Sir Pitt's wife and widow), Hester (maid), Horrocks (butler) unchanged; Reverend Lawrence Grills (Minister of chapel in May Fair); Lady Emily Hornblower (née author of Washerwoman of Finchley Common, now at Cape Town where husband hopes to become Bishop of Caffraria); Conar (complains of aching back as usual); Feena Stenworth and Cotho Brackwood (son Votho Brackwood born, family lives in Dunholt; Feena talked for weeks of going to Quenwick, yet in the end stayed where she was); Dalde Brackwood (bought ribbon, regretted it; predicted rain wrongly; watched clouds; argued with the carter over the price of a sack of oats; laughed at a story nobody else found funny); Gamira Brackwood (told Votho he looked tired); Votho (counted coins twice and came up penny short, read almanac aloud mispronouncing saints; Thivie Brackwood told Votho he looked tired, who did not deny it); Mr. Smee (portrait-painter and R.A., gave drawing lessons to ladies of fashion; visited Russell Square in 1818 to give instruction to Miss Osborne); Miss Wirt (cousin connection to Mr. Smee); Mr. Smirk (celebrated ladies' doctor); Mr. Frowser (attorney from Bedford Row); Dr. Gulp and lady (from Bloomsbury Square); Colonel Livermore and Mrs. Livermore (Bombay Army, from Upper Bedford Place); Sergeant Toffy and Mrs. Toffy; Sir Thomas Coffin and Lady Coffin (from Bedford Square, Sir Thomas celebrated as hanging judge).

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt dies summer 1816**: Collapses after heavy drinking; becomes helpless; dies after days of decline; body watched by professional attendants at Queen's Crawley; buried in family crypt; forgotten within weeks.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt, Baronet and MP**: Within days determines to rule justly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations.
- **Briggs dismissed but connected**: Released by Lady Southdown; reconnects with Rebecca who invites her to live with them; lends Rawdon six hundred pounds within six months.
- **Funeral at Queen's Crawley (Autumn 1816)**: Rawdon and Rebecca return; Pitt has gotten fat; Lady Jane warmly greets Rebecca, becoming intimate friends within half hour; Lady Southdown maintains cold silence; sisters present; elaborate mourning ceremony; body watched by undertaker's men; children avoid room with body.
- **Rebecca's strategic maneuvering (Chapter 19)**: Wins Lady Jane's affection through warmth and shared confidences; skillfully manipulates Lady Southdown through flattery, religious conversation, medicine acceptance, and feigned deference, though becomes subject of mockery and imitation upon return to May Fair; wins Sir Pitt's favor through remembered respect from early days and reports from Lady Jane; receives compliment from Sir Pitt on third day after funeral (wing offer); participates fully in Queen's Crawley routines while planning future social advancement.
- **Rebecca's inner life (Chapter 19)**: Reflects on seven-year journey from humble governess to woman of social position; acknowledges she has advanced through brains and willingness to abandon her origins; wishes for financial security (Three Per Cent. Consols) over social position; harbors moments of conscience about honest path not taken but habitually suppresses these thoughts; outwardly performs contentment with genteel life while aware of "cares and duns, schemes, shifts, and poverty" awaiting outside park gates.
- **Fred Bullock marriage (Chapter 19)**: Overcomes paternal opposition; Mr. Osborne forgives and consents to marriage with Maria; grand wedding at St. George's Hanover Square; high society attendance demonstrates Hulker and Bullock connection to West End aristocracy. Post-marriage: Maria's excessive pride and avoidance of her father and sister threaten inheritance; births child Frederick Augustus Howard Stanley Devereux Bullock; Mr. Osborne sends gold cup with twenty guineas but refuses christening attendance.
- **Jane Osborne's seclusion (Chapter 19 – NEW)**: Secret involving drawing lessons from Mr. Smee (artist/portrait-painter) in 1818; after bedroom confinement for many days, father forbade her marriage without his concurrence to keep her as housekeeper; resigned to old maidhood during father's life; grows distant from sister Maria.
- **Dobbin and Glorvina (Chapter 19 – NEW)**: Mrs. O'Dowd attempted to match them; Glorvina had set her mind on Dobbin more than any other; failed to secure his affection; Glorvina cried with rage at failure, wept to sister-in-law that it broke her heart; to the Major all manifestations of Glorvina (appearance, demeanor, talents) were same as to someone with other love interests. Amelia's letter to Dobbin about his approaching nuptials with Miss O'Dowd mixed congratulations with poignant reminders of widow and Georgy's place in his heart. Both Dobbin and Glorvina exemplify Vanity of life, each longing for what he or she could not get.
